sum: ASML's third-quarter figures, released on 14 October, give investors plenty to chew on beyond the next share-price swing. The Dutch chip-equipment maker booked EUR 11.7 billion in revenue and EUR 5.0 billion in net profit for the period, while gross margin came in at 57.5%.

Those numbers matter because they set the bar for everything else. Anyone weighing the stock should watch not just the top line but the company's ability to defend that earnings quality — and management has now raised its full-year 2026 revenue target to between EUR 44 billion and EUR 45 billion, with gross margin expected at around 56% for the year. Hitting that upgraded plan is the first real test.

The demand side offers support. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are reportedly competing for ASML's EUV systems, and the company has warned that planned capacity will not cover customer needs in 2027 and 2028. That points to a strong demand position — provided customers stick to their stated requirements.

There is a wider backdrop, too. Reuters reported that ASML has stepped up its protective measures after its chip-printing technology became a target in the US-China technology conflict. Technological leadership only counts for so much if its protection does not keep pace with its commercial weight, which is why the hardening of that shield deserves attention alongside the profit line.

Closer to home, four trade unions walked away from talks with ASML, according to media reports. New dates have been set: 7 December 2026 for Design & Engineering and 8 March 2027 for IT. The dispute centres on shifted timelines, with unions fearing the revised schedules leave less time to redeploy affected staff. ASML disputes that the changed dates require consultation under the social plan and says it has offered additional measures.

The crux is how much time employees get to move into new roles internally. A workable settlement would need to square the revised project schedules with those redeployment options; whether the extra measures can offset the feared squeeze is the practical question.

sum: ASML Holding reported a record third quarter on October 14 and raised its 2026 sales outlook as artificial intelligence investment pushed semiconductor equipment demand higher. The update, analyzed by Zacks Research on November 9, places capacity expansion at the center of the investment case.

ASML posted third-quarter revenue of 11.7 billion euros and net income of 5.0 billion euros, according to the analysis. Gross margin reached 57.5%, compared with 51.6% a year earlier and 54% in the second quarter. Installed Base Management revenue rose 67.6% year over year to 3.29 billion euros, reflecting strong demand for productivity upgrades to existing systems.

Management now expects full-year 2026 sales of 44 billion euros to 45 billion euros, implying growth of about 36% from 2025, with a gross margin of about 56%. Fourth-quarter sales are forecast at 14.2 billion euros to 15.2 billion euros, including Installed Base Management revenue of about 3.7 billion euros.

The demand outlook is extending beyond the next reporting periods. ASML said customers expect semiconductor supply to remain below demand through at least 2028, driven largely by AI-related investment. Discussions have moved beyond 2027, with substantial order intake for 2028 and customer interest in deliveries during 2029 and 2030.

That visibility also exposes a constraint. ASML had planned roughly 30% additional low-NA EUV and DUV immersion capacity for 2027 and was considering another 30% increase for 2028. Management now expects those plans may not satisfy customer demand and is examining further expansion for 2028 and beyond.

The operating backdrop is strong, but investors still face execution risks. ASML must expand output while coordinating suppliers, maintaining margins and managing export-control exposure. High-NA EUV provides a longer-term growth opportunity, although customer qualification schedules will determine how quickly it contributes to revenue.

ASML's China Exposure Hinges on MATCH Act Loopholes as Buyback Programme Rolls On
sum: ASML investors are juggling two very different storylines this week: a US legislative fight that will determine how much of its China business survives, and a steady drumbeat of share repurchases that puts real cash behind the company's own confidence.

The MATCH Act, introduced in April, has been folded into the US defence budget for fiscal year 2027, according to a Korea Times report. The draft now awaits full Senate deliberation and reconciliation between the House and the Senate. If the Netherlands and Japan align their export controls with Washington's, equipment from ASML and Tokyo Electron could fall within its scope.

One provision would exempt shipments to existing, foreign-operated plants in China — potentially covering Samsung's NAND fab in Xi'an and SK hynix's DRAM and NAND sites in Wuxi and Dalian. Whether servicing work would also be captured remains unresolved. Such carve-outs could shield ASML's business with those facilities, provided they survive into the final statute and the export rules that follow. For shareholders, both the political deal and the precise reach of the rules matter.

The pressure from Washington may stretch further than the bill itself. Media reports suggest the US could push the Netherlands to halt nearly all ASML shipments of chipmaking equipment to China. The MATCH Act would also prod allies toward restricting older DUV tools.

China accounted for 23% of ASML's system sales in the third quarter of 2026, up from 14% in the prior quarter — a reminder of how much is at stake. That regional split covers system sales only, not group revenue.

ASML has never shipped an EUV scanner to China; Dutch authorities blocked those exports in 2019. Older DUV scanners already require a national export licence, so any tightening would hit a segment where deliveries are still possible on approval. Chinese memory makers CXMT and YMTC have reportedly stockpiled enough ASML DUV equipment to cover their expansion plans for the next three years, a hedge against further restrictions.

Alongside the policy noise, ASML disclosed on Monday the repurchase of 422,800 shares for a total of EUR 562,800,515. The transactions, executed last week, fall under the company's 2026–2028 buyback programme.

sum: ASML shares climbed 5.6% on Friday, riding a broad rebound across semiconductor and AI-related names. The move followed Thursday's selloff, when fears of tighter US regulation of AI infrastructure — amplified by recent Democratic election wins — weighed on the sector, alongside concerns about financing costs and stretched valuations. According to Reuters, the October US jobs report, which came in stronger than expected, helped steady the market, and worries about stricter AI-infrastructure oversight began to fade.
That is encouraging as far as it goes. But the durability of the rally depends less on the mood of the market than on whether ASML can keep up with the demand it says is coming.

On October 14, the Dutch chip-equipment maker said its planned delivery capacity for 2027 and 2028 would not fully cover customer demand. That points to a robust demand base — and, at the same time, makes capacity the binding constraint. Some customers have already expressed interest in orders with delivery in 2029 and 2030, according to the company, and ASML is therefore reviewing a further expansion of capacity.

The question for investors is whether ASML can convert that order backlog into additional shipments. More capacity would only be a plus if customers actually take it up; conversely, strong demand would be more economically useful if ASML could serve it. The two sides have to line up.

More tangible than the shifting sector mood is what the company is doing with its own money. ASML reported the repurchase of 346,200 shares for a total of EUR 504,034,449, with the transactions carried out from October 26 to 30 under its existing buyback program. The disclosure, dated November 2, shows the announced framework being filled with actual capital deployment.

That execution is a firmer anchor than a single trading day's sentiment. A buyback program gains weight through shares actually bought back, and that company-specific commitment deserves more attention than the swings between regulatory fear and relief that have been driving short-term valuations.
The bullish case pairs a sustained stabilization of the industry with progress on ASML's delivery capabilities.

sum: Two narratives are colliding around ASML Holding this week, and only one of them will ultimately move the stock.

On one side sits a fresh estimate from ING Research, published October 26, which sizes up just how deeply the Dutch economy leans on the chip-equipment maker. On the other, a familiar pattern of sector-wide turbulence: ASML's US-listed shares were swept into a broad semiconductor selloff on Friday after Intel delivered a disappointing outlook, while investors simultaneously began questioning the returns on the industry's massive AI infrastructure spending. No new operating statement from ASML drove that move — the uncertainty came entirely from the surrounding environment.

Then the picture shifted again. ASML shares climbed 2.1% as chip stocks staged a recovery, with memory and equipment names reportedly leading the rebound following recent steep losses. That bounce, however, is a sector story, not a company story. It offers no fresh evidence that ASML's own business prospects have improved.

The ING Research estimate puts ASML's total economic footprint for 2026 at as much as 2.2% of Dutch gross value added, with the direct contribution potentially reaching 1.6%. Both figures are projections, not settled outcomes.

The gap between the direct contribution and the broader footprint matters. The study isn't only about ASML itself — it flags the Netherlands' growing dependence on the company and on its semiconductor-equipment cluster, turning a corporate success story into a question of economic concentration.

For investors, that pivotal position is an argument for ASML's relevance. It says nothing about what the shares should be worth. Macroeconomic weight and market valuation measure different things, and conflating the two mistakes economic importance for portfolio safety. Friday's session made that distinction plain.

What actually anchors the investment case is the guidance ASML issued roughly three weeks ago. Management projected fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of EUR 14.2 billion to EUR 15.2 billion — the central yardstick against which any lasting recovery must be measured. The update, widely reported in the media, reinforced confidence in AI infrastructure spending, and ASML rode the sector wave. The catalyst came from the market backdrop rather than from any fresh announcement by the Dutch equipment maker — a distinction that matters for anyone reading the move as company-specific news.

Super Micro's guidance concerns its own top line. For ASML, it merely underpins expectations of sustained demand across the chip sector; no new order or revised corporate forecast can be inferred from it. The advance also stands in sharp contrast to the skepticism that gripped the stock as recently as mid-October, when Reuters reported a decline for ASML amid a broader market selloff, citing doubts about the lofty expectations baked into 2028 and 2029.

On the same day, BofA Securities reiterated its buy rating on ASML, pointing to revenue and margin potential as well as possible price increases as drivers. Jefferies analyst Janardan Menon takes a more guarded view: cyclically compressing valuation multiples could cap the upside. For investors, strong demand alone does not settle the question — the price the market is willing to pay for future earnings matters just as much.

The quarterly results published roughly a week ago give the bulls operational ammunition. Gross margin for the third quarter of 2026 came in at 57.5%, and the business built on ASML's installed machine base contributed EUR 3.289 billion, or 28.2% of revenue. Upgrades to existing systems propped up margins, which means earnings do not hinge solely on how many new tools leave the factory — retrofitting machines already in the field carries real weight.

Management's guidance offers a concrete yardstick for the margin case BofA is making. For the closing quarter of 2026, ASML projected service revenue of around EUR 3.7 billion and a full-year gross margin of roughly 56%. ASML's extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines are used to print the most complex circuits in leading-edge chips. As chipmakers pack more computing power into smaller chips, they need more precise manufacturing equipment. This trend has been driving demand for ASML's systems.

Applied Materials is also playing a crucial role in manufacturing advanced chips. sum: Shares of ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) were pulling back last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks and as the company reported second-quarter earnings, which briefly lifted the stock, though that wasn't enough to drive gains over the course of the month.

According to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, the stock finished the month down 18%. sum: China's breakthrough in domestic chipmaking equipment sparked a major semiconductor sell-off, dragging down Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) despite strong fundamentals.

An announcement from a manufacturing facility in Shanghai on July 27, 2026, caused a severe summer downturn for the AI semiconductor market. State-supported Shanghai Aishengna reported the production of homegrown immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems for domestic fabrication facilities. It marks the first viable domestic substitute for technology ASML (NASDAQ:ASML) has exclusively controlled for twenty years, leading to an 8% decline in ASML's shares. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) fell over 8%, recording the steepest decline among its peers. The fall comes despite the core business metrics remaining steady. Immersion DUV technology processes mature nodes. On the other hand, AMD's MI300 series and upcoming MI400/MI455X accelerators rely on TSMC's cutting-edge extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. As such, their technology affects neither TSMC's supply chain nor AMD's pricing power. Additionally, Aishengna aims for just five units in 2026 compared to ASML's 130 in the same year. With EUV remaining inaccessible to domestic producers, investors' reaction is impulsive rather than based on an evaluation of the underlying technical reality.

The numbers remain solid even after the decline. Post-drop, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) is trading near a forward P/E of 60 – approximately two times the industry median of 30x. Its EV/EBITDA is in the upper 80s, and its PEG is above 1.2 as compared to Nvidia at 0.5.

sum: The evaporation of massive market value due to an industrial report shows that Western investors' blind faith in the effectiveness of "blockades" has been shaken, and the US-led "decoupling" strategy has lost much of its momentum. One day, the technologies once used to constrain China's development will simply become ordinary components of its independent industrial system.

An industrial report by US tech media regarding a breakthrough in China's domestic lithography development sent shockwaves through global stock markets between Monday and Tuesday. From Europe and the US to Japan and South Korea, companies tied to the global chip equipment supply chain saw their stock prices drop, with Dutch lithography giant ASML taking a "hit" of roughly 7 percent on Monday. That an unconfirmed report could trigger such violent market volatility illustrates current paranoia of some forces in the West regarding China's technological rise.

The evaporation of massive market value shows that Western investors' blind faith in the effectiveness of "blockades" has been shaken, and the US-led "decoupling" strategy has lost much of its momentum. Though they may not admit it openly, they know in their hearts that a Chinese breakthrough in "chokepoint" technologies is merely a matter of time.

In recent years, the US has strengthened the implementation of the Wassenaar Arrangement, which imposes technology controls on other countries, to repeatedly impose restrictions and sanctions on China's high-tech sectors while pressuring its allies into a "chip alliance," all aimed at severing China's access to advanced technologies. However, they have overlooked a fundamental truth: Technological blockades are always mutually destructive. By locking others out, one also forfeits the market and space for cooperation. China boasts the world's largest semiconductor consumption market, backed by a complete industrial system and a vast pool of engineers - conditions that guarantee Western blockades will not succeed in the long run. Even Western tech companies like ASML understand that once China achieves a genuine breakthrough, their market share will face a direct hit.

The move followed a report from The Information that an unnamed state-backed Chinese manufacturer has started building these systems. However, Wall Street, as well as retail investors, dismissed the selloff.
Initial reported plans call for roughly five machines this year and about 20 in 2027, far below ASML's output of 131 immersion DUV systems last year, it said.

sum: The Dutch company plans to issue the share award on January 1, with full vesting occurring at the start of 2030 for those who stay with ASML through that date, the firm confirmed in an emailed statement on Friday, July 17. A spokesperson said that the bonus is intended to recognize "the extraordinary efforts and contributions of our teams during a period of exceptional growth."

With 45,000 employees, the total cost of the bonus is approximately €900 million - a significant but manageable expense given ASML's record revenues. The award also signals confidence in the company's future trajectory, as it expects continued robust demand from AI chipmakers.

The core objective of SK Hynix's fundraising is clear: all proceeds will be invested in expanding production capacity in South Korea, including upgrading advanced packaging facilities and large-scale purchases of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment from Dutch equipment giant ASML. The market interpreted this as a clearer timeline for large-scale equipment procurement, further reinforcing optimistic expectations for EUV equipment demand and semiconductor capital expenditure.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: The world's largest foundry company

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +6.33%), popularly known as TSMC, is the world's largest semiconductor foundry that manufactures chips designed by fabless chipmakers. The Taiwan-based company doesn't design its own chips. Instead, it is involved in the mass production of chips for companies such as Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Sony, and others, who don't have their own chipmaking facilities.

ASML, which is based in the Netherlands, is the world's largest producer of lithography machines for optically etching circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. It's also the only producer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, which the world's top foundries -- including TSMC and Samsung -- use to manufacture their most advanced chips.

ASML's EUV systems, which cost $200 million to $400 million, require multiple planes to ship. As a linchpin of the global semiconductor industry, it has tremendous pricing power and an impenetrable moat. That's why its gross margin rose from 48.6% in 2020 to 52.8% in 2025.

From 2020 to 2025, its revenue and EPS grew at CAGRs of 18% and 24%, respectively. It achieved that growth even as the pandemic, supply chain disruptions, inflation, rising interest rates, geopolitical conflicts, and other macro headwinds rattled the global economy.

ASML kept growing because the world's top foundries must keep installing its lithography systems to stay competitive. In the past, its growth was pegged to the semiconductor market's boom-and-bust cycles. But over the past few years, its growth has been driven by surging demand for GPUs, memory chips, and custom networking chips in the booming AI market.

All of those chipmakers need to use ASML's EUV systems -- whether at their third-party foundries or first-party plants -- to manufacture their smallest and densest chips. That makes ASML one of the easiest ways to profit from the semiconductor sector's long-term expansion without investing too heavily in a single chipmaker. It also makes ASML an evergreen stock.

From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect ASML's revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 18% and 27%, respectively, as the AI boom continues. It will sell more of its newest high-NA EUV systems, which are used to produce the world's most powerful chips, as well as a steady stream of its older low-NA EUV systems and deep ultraviolet (DUV) systems for mature nodes.

items.t: 1 Prediction for ASML Stock in 2026
sum: It can be fun, and occasionally instructive, to see what some people predict for various stocks. So permit me to make a prediction: In 2026, ASML (ASML +6.33%) will thrive.

The company specializes in making the lithography equipment required for semiconductor manufacturing, and it's the only provider of advanced extreme ultraviolet systems (EUVs) -- which my colleague James Hires has called "the most important machine in tech."

ASML's equipment etches intricate circuitry onto tiny silicon wafers. Such equipment is very pricey, with its EUV machines costing around $400 million apiece. Better still, ASML's machines tend to last for decades, and throughout that period, they require servicing and occasional parts replacement -- from ASML.
It's no wonder, then, that the company has been thriving, posting average annual gains of 30% over the past decade (as of March 23). Over the past year, its stock has surged nearly 80%.

I'm predicting that ASML will keep thriving because semiconductor companies will keep thriving, as they're vital for artificial intelligence (AI). A select group of huge tech companies is investing heavily in AI -- to the tune of nearly $700 billion in 2026 alone.

That's reflected to some degree in ASML's fourth-quarter earnings report, which featured a backlog of orders totaling 38.8 billion euros (nearly $45 billion at recent conversion rates). Its CEO has noted that "...we expect 2026 to be another growth year for ASML's business, largely driven by a significant increase in EUV sales..."

Of course, there are some risks, including geopolitical ones. If it's less able to do business with China, for example, that will hurt. And regardless of that, ASML will need to keep innovating and improving its offerings in order to receive more orders.

ASML's customers are moving from 4 nanometers (nm) to 3nm, and some are also ramping 2nm. The transition to advanced nodes requires more EUV layers and higher precision and is driving the demand for ASML's High-NA EUV tools. At the same time, AI demand is driving capacity expansion in logic and memory. ASML noted that its customers have become more confident about long-term AI demand and are increasing investment plans. From a financial standpoint, EUV remains the main growth driver. Bookings at the end of the fourth quarter were €13.2 billion, out of which €7.4 billion was from EUV. sum: The arithmetic of ASML's capital returns is hard to ignore. items.t: ASML's Revenue Mix is Changing: What are the Latest Growth Drivers?
sum: ASML Holding ASML completed its 2025 results with €32.67 billion, up 15.6% year over year. ASML's net systems sales contributed 74.9% of the top line, up 12.4% year over year. ASML's net systems sales saw a decline in contribution from China. China contributed 41% to net systems sales in 2024 and 33% in 2025.

The decline was mainly due to U.S.-led export restrictions combined with demand normalization following high deep ultraviolet (DUV) equipment demand in 2024. However, the gap was filled by South Korea and Taiwan, which contributed 25% and 22% in 2025, up from 21% and 11%, respectively, in the year-ago quarter.

On the technology side, extreme ultraviolet (EUV) technology is expanding its contribution to the top line, replacing DUV. EUV contributed 48% to the net systems sales, up from the contribution of 38% in 2024. The demand for EUV is rising proportionately with the growing usage of AI chips, as foundries have to transition to 3nm / 2nm nodes requiring more EUV layers per chip.

The rise in demand for memory products like high bandwidth memory and DDR is also causing traction in EUV technology. As the world moves toward sub-2nm manufacturing, the demand for High-NA EUV systems will also rise, giving ASML a multi-year runway for harnessing growth, as evident in the €38.8 billion backlog in the year ended 2025.
ASML competes with companies like Lam Research LRCX and Applied Materials AMAT in the wafer fabrication equipment (WFE) space.

Lam Research is an established WFE manufacturer that is established in the memory space. Lam Research's memory segment, accounting for both Dynamic Random Access Memory and Non-Volatile Memory divisions, is gaining traction on the back of AI.

Applied Materials supplies equipment used in chip fabrication, including deposition and etching tools that are essential for both advanced and mature nodes. As chips become more complex with AI and high-performance workloads, Applied Materials' tools aid in designing and making efficient and smaller node chips.

Nonetheless, ASML's equipment is critical to AI, meaning it will probably take more than a high valuation and a lack of name recognition to stop its growth.

items.t: Could Investing $10,000 in ASML Make You a Millionaire?
sum: Most experienced investors understand that life-changing stocks come from world-changing companies. Think Amazon, or, more recently, Nvidia. The former arguably created the e-commerce industry it now dominates, while the latter's technology is the heart and soul of most artificial intelligence platforms. That's why so many of these two outfits' earliest shareholders were able to turn relatively modest investments into million-dollar positions.
Not every critical technology company makes for a life-changing stock, though. Sometimes, their tickers are merely better-than-average performers.

And this is a question that may be on investors' minds regarding ASML Holding (ASML -0.36%) right now. It's a hugely important semiconductor technology outfit. But, is it a millionaire-making prospect with nothing more than a fairly typical investment of $10,000 made today?

Have you ever wondered how semiconductor chips are made? There's actually more than one way. The most common way, however, is with light. Using a manufacturing process known as lithography, a light-based stencil (of sorts) is used to spray multiple layers of semiconducting material onto a silicon substrate. The more precise this light pattern is, the smaller the chips made with it can be.

One company dominates this market -- Netherlands-based ASML. Protected by tens of thousands of the right patents, this company controls most of the overall lithography market, and almost the entirety of the extreme ultraviolet (or EUV) lithography industry, and is responsible for making the world's highest-performance computer chips. You may know that Taiwan Semiconductor is the world's single biggest manufacturer of high-performance silicon. Well, for perspective, Taiwan Semiconductor is ASML's biggest customer.

It's doing well, too. In 2024, the chipmaking technology powerhouse generated $33 billion in revenue, translating to a net income of $8.8 billion, a notable increase for the former but a slight decline for the latter. Still, that's a smashing success.
The question remains, however, could investing $10,000 in this company today turn you into a millionaire at any point in your lifetime?

items.t: What To Expect From ASML In 2026?
sum: ASML (NASDAQ: ASML), the Dutch semiconductor equipment leader and monopoly supplier of EUV lithography, kicks off 2026 on a strong note. After a turbulent 2025, the stock has surged nearly 16% in the first week of January, fueled by a flurry of analyst upgrades and price targets reaching as high as $1,500. Here are the pivotal trends that could shape ASML’s outlook this year.

The semiconductor industry has officially entered the High-NA (Numerical Aperture) EUV era. These next-generation lithography machines are the most complex and expensive manufacturing tools ever built, costing roughly $380 million per system. Their importance goes far beyond price. High-NA EUV enables chipmakers to print features roughly twice as small as today’s EUV systems, making it essential for future nodes such as 1.4 nm and eventually 1 nm. Without High-NA, continued transistor scaling for advanced AI processors becomes economically and technically unviable.

Adoption will move from theory to reality. Intel has completed acceptance testing for its first High-NA systems intended for mass production, while Samsung has begun taking delivery for its upcoming 2nm foundry lines. Although the cost of these machines is high, their technical necessity in the AI arms race is forcing leading-edge manufacturers to commit. For ASML, this marks a structural shift toward a higher-margin, longer-duration revenue stream. No competing company can build these tools, making High-NA EUV one of the strongest competitive moats in industrial history. This could effectively lock in ASML’s relevance for the next decade.

China has been one of ASML’s largest customers recently, accounting for over 40% of sales during 2024–2025. That demand surge, however, was driven by stockpiling as Chinese chipmakers rushed to acquire tools and machinery ahead of expanding export controls. In 2026, that cycle has clearly turned. Tighter Dutch and U.S. restrictions now limit shipments not only of advanced EUV systems but also high-end DUV immersion tools. As a result, Chinese revenue is expected to decline meaningfully this year, creating what could be a temporary “air pocket” in regional sales.

Prices fluctuate constantly, so traders generally monitor live data from their broker or a dedicated financial information service.

A stock split is a corporate action that increases the number of shares in circulation while reducing the price per share proportionally. The company’s market capitalisation doesn’t change at the moment of the split, and shareholders maintain the same economic interest.

In a 2-for-1 split, for instance, each share becomes two shares and the share price adjusts to roughly half its previous level. While the price changes, the company’s revenue, earnings and other fundamentals remain unchanged. Splits are often used to support liquidity or keep the share price within a range that feels more accessible to a broader investor base.
